subject: Geography
description: Igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic rocks; rock cycle; common minerals; ores

questions.stem: Rocks formed by the cooling and solidification of MAGMA or LAVA are called:

options.option_text: Sedimentary rocks, formed by deposition of sediments over time
Igneous rocks, formed when molten material cools and solidifies
Metamorphic rocks, formed under heat and pressure
Loose sediments, like sand and clay layers in deltas

questions.explanation: IGNEOUS rocks (Latin 'ignis' fire) — cooled magma (intrusive, slow-cooled, large crystals — granite) or lava (extrusive, fast-cooled, small crystals — basalt). The Deccan Traps are basalt flows (~65 million years old). SEDIMENTARY (Distractor 1) — formed by accumulation + cementation of particles (sandstone, limestone). METAMORPHIC (Distractor 3) — pre-existing rocks transformed by heat / pressure (limestone → marble, shale → slate, granite → gneiss).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: MARBLE is the metamorphic form of which sedimentary rock?

options.option_text: Sandstone, formed from compacted sand grains
Limestone, formed mainly from calcium carbonate
Shale, a fine-grained clay-rich rock
Conglomerate, a coarse rock of rounded pebbles

questions.explanation: Marble = metamorphosed LIMESTONE (CaCO₃). Heat + pressure recrystallise the calcite grains into a denser, harder rock. Famous Indian marbles — Makrana (Rajasthan), used in Taj Mahal. Other parent → metamorphic pairs: SANDSTONE → quartzite; SHALE → slate (then phyllite, schist, gneiss with increasing grade); GRANITE → gneiss; LIMESTONE → marble; coal → graphite → diamond (with extreme P + T).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The most ABUNDANT element in the Earth's continental crust by weight is:

options.option_text: Iron, the major component of Earth's core
Oxygen, present in nearly all silicate minerals
Carbon, the basis of life and organic compounds
Hydrogen, the lightest and most common in oceans

questions.explanation: Earth's crust composition (by mass): Oxygen ~46%, Silicon ~28%, Aluminium ~8%, Iron ~5%, Calcium ~4%, Sodium ~3%, Potassium ~3%, Magnesium ~2%, others ~1%. Most rock-forming minerals are SILICATES (containing SiO₄ tetrahedra) — quartz, feldspar, mica, pyroxene, amphibole. Iron is abundant in the CORE but only ~5% of the crust. Distractor 1 confuses crust with core. Distractor 3 — carbon is rare in crust (~0.1%). Distractor 4 — hydrogen is abundant in oceans/atmosphere but minor in crust.

questions.stem: The hardest naturally-occurring substance — a 10 on the Mohs scale — is:

options.option_text: Quartz, found in many sedimentary rocks
Diamond, the high-pressure form of carbon
Corundum, the gem family with sapphire and ruby
Topaz, a silicate gemstone of pale colour

questions.explanation: Mohs hardness scale (1-10): TALC 1, GYPSUM 2, CALCITE 3, FLUORITE 4, APATITE 5, ORTHOCLASE FELDSPAR 6, QUARTZ 7, TOPAZ 8, CORUNDUM 9, DIAMOND 10. Diamond is the hardest known natural substance (carbon atoms in tetrahedral covalent network). Synthetic substances — wurtzite boron nitride, lonsdaleite — even harder. Mineral hardness measures resistance to scratching, not toughness (diamond can shatter from impact). Industrial diamond is used in cutting tools, drill bits, abrasives.

questions.stem: The major ORE of ALUMINIUM is:

options.option_text: Hematite, an iron-rich red ore mineral
Bauxite, a hydrated aluminium oxide ore
Galena, the chief lead-bearing mineral
Cinnabar, the principal mercury ore

questions.explanation: BAUXITE — Al₂O₃·xH₂O (hydrated aluminium oxide). Major aluminium ore. Refined to alumina via the Bayer process; alumina then electrolysed (Hall-Héroult process) to yield aluminium. India is among the top 5 bauxite producers; major reserves in Odisha (Panchpatmali, Kalahandi), AP, Jharkhand, Gujarat, Maharashtra. Distractor 1 — hematite is iron ore (Fe₂O₃). Distractor 3 — galena is lead ore (PbS). Distractor 4 — cinnabar is mercury ore (HgS). Other ore-element pairs to know: pyrite/iron, magnetite/iron, chalcopyrite/copper, sphalerite/zinc, monazite/thorium-rare earths.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: BASALT, the dark volcanic rock that covers much of the Deccan plateau, is an:

options.option_text: Intrusive coarse-grained igneous rock cooling slowly underground
Extrusive fine-grained igneous rock from cooling lava on the surface
Sedimentary rock made of compacted volcanic ash and dust
Metamorphic rock formed from limestone under intense pressure

questions.explanation: BASALT — extrusive (volcanic), mafic, fine-grained because it cools rapidly when erupted onto the surface. Deccan Traps in central + western India: ~65 million years ago, vast lava flows from a hot-spot eruption (linked to the K-Pg mass extinction along with the Chicxulub impact). Cover ~500,000 km², forming distinctive 'trap' (staircase) topography in Maharashtra, Gujarat, MP. Also major in mid-ocean ridges, oceanic crust, ocean islands like Hawaii. Distractor 1 = granite (intrusive felsic). Distractor 3 = tuff. Distractor 4 = marble.
questions.subject: Geography

options.option_text: Rocks remain unchanged in their original form indefinitely
Each rock type can transform into the others over geological time
Sedimentary rocks are formed only at the equator regions
Igneous rocks always remain igneous after their formation

questions.explanation: Rock cycle — geological process by which the three rock types interconvert: IGNEOUS rocks weather and erode → sediments → SEDIMENTARY rocks; sedimentary rocks subjected to heat + pressure → METAMORPHIC; metamorphic rocks melt → magma → IGNEOUS again. Time scale — typically millions of years. Driving forces: plate tectonics, volcanism, weathering, erosion, deposition. Sedimentary rocks form anywhere sediments accumulate (river deltas, sea floors, lakebeds, deserts) — NOT just at the equator.

questions.stem: A freshly quarried piece of granite shows clearly visible crystals of quartz, feldspar, and mica to the naked eye. This coarse-grained texture forms because the parent magma:

options.option_text: Erupted as lava and cooled very rapidly at the Earth's surface
Cooled slowly deep underground, allowing large crystals to grow
Was compressed under immense pressure without any heat involved
Underwent repeated melting cycles inside a shallow volcanic vent

questions.explanation: B is correct because granite is a plutonic (intrusive) igneous rock; slow cooling kilometres underground gives ions time to migrate and form large, interlocking crystals. Option A describes extrusive rocks like basalt, where rapid cooling at or near the surface produces fine-grained or glassy textures — no visible crystals.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs CORRECTLY matches a rock with its primary formation process?

options.option_text: Limestone — accumulation and compression of marine shell and coral debris
Quartzite — slow cooling of silica-rich magma in underground chambers
Gabbro — layering of wind-blown sand grains cemented over millennia
Schist — rapid solidification of iron-rich lava on the ocean floor

questions.explanation: A is correct: limestone is a biochemical sedimentary rock built from calcium carbonate skeletons of marine organisms. Quartzite is metamorphic (sandstone recrystallised under heat and pressure), Gabbro is a coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock, and Schist is a foliated metamorphic rock derived from shale — none involve sedimentation of shells.

questions.stem: Kodarma in Jharkhand is called India's 'Mica Capital.' The commercially dominant variety mined there — prized for electrical insulation and capacitor manufacturing — is:

options.option_text: Biotite mica — dark brown, iron and magnesium-rich silicate mineral
Muscovite mica — colourless, potassium-rich, with high dielectric strength
Lepidolite mica — violet-hued, lithium-bearing, used mainly in ceramics
Phlogopite mica — amber-coloured, magnesium-rich, stable at high heat

questions.explanation: B is correct: Muscovite (potassium aluminium mica) is the commercial-grade mica of the Kodarma–Giridih belt; its transparency and exceptional electrical resistance make it ideal for insulators and capacitors. Biotite (Option A) is dark and electrically conductive — unsuitable for insulation; Phlogopite and Lepidolite are mined elsewhere for different uses.

questions.stem: Laterite rock, widespread across the Western Ghats and parts of the Deccan, acquires its distinctive brick-red colour primarily due to the concentration of:

options.option_text: Aluminium hydroxide (Al(OH)₃), the chief mineral component of bauxite
Iron oxides (Fe₂O₃/Fe₃O₄), left behind after silica is leached away
Manganese dioxide (MnO₂), deposited by oxidising groundwater seepage
Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), precipitated during intense tropical weathering

questions.explanation: B is correct: intense tropical leaching strips soluble silica and bases, leaving insoluble iron oxides (haematite Fe₂O₃ and goethite) that colour laterite red. Option A is the basis of bauxite — a related but geochemically distinct product where aluminium hydroxides dominate instead; bauxite tends to be white or cream-coloured, not red.

questions.stem: The Gondwana coalfields, which hold over 98% of India's coal reserves, were deposited during which geological period?

options.option_text: Carboniferous period (360–300 Ma) — when Europe's great coal forests thrived
Permian period (300–252 Ma) — when Gondwanaland's swamp forests flourished
Jurassic period (201–145 Ma) — coinciding with dinosaur-era dense vegetation
Cretaceous period (145–66 Ma) — marked by rapid flowering-plant expansion

questions.explanation: B is correct: Gondwana coal is Permian in age, formed when the Gondwanaland supercontinent bore extensive forested swamps; India was part of this landmass. Option A (Carboniferous) applies to European and North American coalfields — a classic exam trap, since students associate coal generally with the Carboniferous era without knowing India's coal is specifically Permian.

questions.stem: India's only mechanised diamond mine at Panna (Madhya Pradesh) extracts diamonds from kimberlite pipe intrusions. Kimberlite is best classified as which rock type?

options.option_text: Felsic extrusive igneous rock, compositionally similar to rhyolite lava
Ultramafic igneous rock emplaced from mantle depths exceeding 150 km
High-grade metamorphic rock recrystallised under upper-mantle conditions
Carbonatite intrusive rock formed in ancient alkaline deep-crustal settings

questions.explanation: B is correct: kimberlite is an ultramafic, volatile-rich igneous rock (very low silica, high Mg/Fe) explosively intruded from depths of 150–200 km — the only pressure-temperature regime where diamonds are thermodynamically stable. Option C is a common trap; while diamonds require mantle conditions, kimberlite itself is igneous (solidified melt), not metamorphic. Option A is wrong because kimberlite is silica-poor, the opposite of felsic rocks like rhyolite.

questions.stem: Pumice is the only common rock that floats on water when freshly erupted. The CORRECT physical explanation for this property is:

options.option_text: Its silica content exceeds 75%, drastically reducing its molecular density
Rapid vesiculation traps gas pockets, making bulk density fall below 1 g/cm³
Iron oxidation during eruption converts dense magnetite to light haematite
The glassy amorphous silica network in pumice actively repels polar water molecules

questions.explanation: B is correct: during explosive eruptions, dissolved volcanic gases (H₂O, CO₂, SO₂) rapidly exsolve as lava decompresses, creating a foam of countless tiny vesicles; these gas voids lower pumice's bulk density to 0.25–0.9 g/cm³ — less than water's 1 g/cm³. Option A is the most tempting distractor: obsidian is also high-silica (>70%) but has no vesicles and sinks readily, proving silica content alone is irrelevant to buoyancy.
